messages.subject: Saving Map
messages.body_plain:
Dear Professor,

I am trying to save the genetic map with genotype information in csv file using the following codes-

  mycross <- replace.map(mycross, mymap)
  mymapAsTable <- pull.map(mymap, as.table=TRUE)
  write.csv(mymapAsTable, file="mymap.csv")

But from this I am getting the csv file only with marker positions (please see attached file). But for QTL mapping I need the genotype information of each marker in this map as well. Is there any code by which I can  do so?

Many thanks in advance.

Best regards,
Mehedi

Use write.cross:

  write.cross(mycross, "csv", "mycross")

Would it be okay for me to post your question and my response to the R/qtl discussion group? (http://groups.google.com/group/Rqtl-disc)
I prefer to have R/qtl correspondence through there, so that others may benefit.

karl

messages.subject: Imputation
messages.body_plain:
Hello

I was wondering is it possible to use haley knott regression method to impute the missing data in r/QTL. Because I need the imputed data for MCMC analysis.

thanks,

Boby Mathew
messages.body_snippet:
Hello

I was wondering is it possible to use haley knott regression method to impute the missing data in r/QTL. Because I need the imputed data for MCMC analysis.

thanks,

Boby Mathew

messages.subject: Re: Imputation
messages.body_plain:
Haley-Knott regression is a method for QTL analysis; I can't think of a way that it can be used as a method to impute missing data.

To impute missing genotype data, use fill.geno(). There are three options:

  - "imp": take a random draw from Pr(genotype | marker data)
  - "argmax": choose the sequence of genotypes for which Pr(genotypes | marker data) is maximal
  - "no_dbl_XO": missing values between two matching genotypes (non-recombinant) are filled in with that match; missing values between recombinant genotypes are left missing

karl

messages.subject: Re: Imputation
messages.body_plain:
In the development version of R/qtl, I've added a new option for fill.geno, method="maxmarginal". At each marker, it picks the genotype with maximum probability (provided this exceeds a chosen threshold, min.prob).
>

The key code is at https://github.com/kbroman/qtl/blob/devel/R/util.R#L1858-L1867

You could do this "by hand" as follows:

temp <- calc.genoprob(cross, error.prob=0.01)

for(i in 1:n.chr) {
    p <- temp$geno[[i]]$prob
    whmax <- apply(p, 1:2, which.max)
    maxpr <- apply(p, 1:2, max)
    g <- cross$geno[[i]]$data
    g[maxpr > min.prob] <- whmax[maxpr > min.prob]
    cross$geno[[i]]$data <- g
}

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Re: X'X matrix is singular.
messages.body_plain:
The problem is similar to the "X'X is singular problem"; an issue in fitting the logistic regression model. Usually these issues occur in regions where there's no evidence for a QTL anyway, so they can generally be ignored.

Look at a plot of the LOD curves. If there are extremely high LOD score, be suspicious. If things look reasonable, then don't worry.

karl

messages.subject: Marker density problems
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl et al.
This question may have been asked before... I am sure the problem plagues any of us using maps from NGS genotyping.

I have a RAD genotyped population with ~4000 markers (its a BIG map w/ 2600 total cM). Many of these markers are in close proximity (as many as 8/cM).
To speed up QTL mapping, I have culled the map to include only a single marker / cM, and this works fine, but I am wondering if there is a better or more computationally efficient way to set up the map. What do you think about dropping all markers and using only the pseudomarkers for the analysis?

Any advice is appreciated!
John

John Lovell
Postdoc, UT Austin, USA.

messages.subject: R/qtl version 1.34-16
messages.body_plain:
A new version of R/qtl (1.34-16) has been released at its web site
(http://www.rqtl.org) and will soon appear on CRAN.

There are a bunch of major changes:

  Added scanonevar() function, for a single-QTL genome scan for QTL
  affecting not just the mean phenotype but also the variance. (Code
  from Lars Ronnegard; method in Ronnegard and Valdar Genetics
  188:435-447, 2011.)

  Added ability to do X-chr-specific permutations in scantwo (argument
  perm.Xsp, as in scanone). Separate thresholds are obtained for the
  regions A:A, A:X, and X:X regions, maintaining control of the
  overall false positive rates.

  Added a function scantwopermhk that just performs scantwo
  permutations with Haley-Knott regression; faster and with lower
  memory usage than scantwo.

  With X-chr-specific scantwo permutations, calc.penalties will give
  separate main effect for autosome and X chromosome, and separate
  interaction penalties for A:A, A:X, X:X. For A:A interactions, we
  still use "light" and "heavy" penalties; for A:X and X:X
  interactions, only the "heavy" penalty is used. These penalties may
  be used in stepwiseqtl for better treatment of the X chromosome in
  automated inference of multi-QTL models.

  Added "tidy" format to read.cross and write.cross. This separates
  the data into three comma-delimited files, for genotypes,
  phenotypes, and the marker map. Separating the data in this way
  allows each file to be in a simpler format.

A complete list of changes is at http://rqtl.org/STATUS.txt

Karl Broman

messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,

I realize that I was not clear at all, sorry. I am trying to figure out what would be the best way to form linkage groups from a dataset with around 45,000 markers, in a population of the ri self or f2 intercross type (typically 200 individuals). The problem is that our datasets (GBS) usually contain plenty of missing data (ranging from 25 to 65 %), so I can't see how findDupMarkers and find duplicates efficiently.

Also, the markers are not ordered a priori since we don't have a reference genome.

My understanding is that in R/qtl it is necessary to compute the LOD score/recombination fraction matrix before forming the linkage groups. And on my machine (64 bit, 16 GB RAM), this take a so huge amount of RAM that R starts swapping on the hard drive and I expect this to last for ages (I calculated that the LOD/recombination fraction matrix' size would be around 65 GB).

So I was wondering if it would be possible to form the linkage groups without computing the entire matrix, for example, one could compute only the recombination fraction and LOD score for the tested pair of markers.

Does this make sense to you?

Thanks very much for the support.

All the best,
Mathias
